title: Nonprofit infrastructure is widely used but institutionally unrecognized, weakening the public service bargain
source_unit: Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, What Americans Think About Nonprofits & Philanthropy 2026, September 25, 2026
geography: United States; adults in the national survey summarized by Indiana University

denominator.unit: respondents in the 2026 national report; sample size is not stated in the public IU news release

self_identified_nonprofit_use.unit: percent reporting that they or an immediate family member received or used charitable-organization services in the past year

activity_typically_provided_by_nonprofit.unit: percent reporting at least one activity typically provided by nonprofits

recognition_gap.value: Nearly 90% of people whose reported activities fit nonprofit service use did not initially identify themselves as nonprofit users

mechanism.value: Social infrastructure can be widely consumed as ordinary community life while remaining institutionally invisible to the people who rely on it

observations.method: IU public release summarizing the 2026 What Americans Think About Nonprofits & Philanthropy report, which builds on 2023 research; the public release does not state the survey sample size or full instrument.
observations.uncertainty: The activity list, wording, field dates, sampling frame and classification rules are not fully reproduced in the public release; reported activity does not establish service quality, intensity, access, unmet need or causal recognition effects.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults and households using services or activities associated with nonprofits, potentially varying by income, race, disability, geography, faith, household composition and service type; subgroup estimates are not supplied in the release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may distinguish formal charitable services from community activities for reasons of wording or identity, and low recognition does not necessarily mean low appreciation or support for nonprofits.

observations.period: 2026; nonprofit confidence, institutional influence and political signaling

high_confidence_solving_problems.unit: percent expressing high confidence in nonprofits' ability to solve societal or global problems

political_trust_sensitivity.unit: percent saying their confidence in nonprofits would decrease if a trusted political figure expressed a lack of confidence in the sector

sector_direction_uncertainty.unit: percent saying they did not know whether the nonprofit and philanthropic sector was headed in the right direction or wrong track

mechanism.value: Nonprofit legitimacy is comparatively strong but conditional: public confidence can be shaped by political intermediaries even when everyday use is under-recognized

observations.method: IU report summary comparing nonprofit confidence, political-figure influence and perceived sector direction in 2026.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported attitudes, not institutional-performance measures, donation behavior, policy compliance or observed political influence; the release does not identify causal pathways.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults with different political identities, nonprofit experiences, media exposure and institutional trust; subgroup estimates are not reported in the public release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Political statements may be proxies for broader news, ideology or prior confidence rather than direct causes of trust change; uncertainty may reflect lack of information rather than ambivalence.

observations.period: 2026 compared with 2023; provider roles, giving expectations and institutional design

denominator.unit: respondents in the 2026 report and comparable 2023 report items

nonprofit_better_than_government_basic_n.unit: percent saying nonprofits are more effective than government at providing basic needs, down from 24.6% in 2023

universal_charitable_deduction_giving_in.unit: percent saying their giving would increase because of the enacted universal charitable deduction, down from 24.4% in the 2023 report's comparison

foundation_perpetuity_preference.unit: percent preferring foundations to reserve assets to give over time or in perpetuity, versus 21.3% preferring rapid distribution

mechanism.value: Institutional design is judged through service availability, provider roles and time horizon; public support for nonprofit infrastructure does not imply a simple preference for nonprofit rather than government provision

observations.method: IU release reporting 2026 measures and selected comparisons with the 2023 report; the public release does not provide full question wording, weights, sample details or harmonization documentation.
observations.uncertainty: Changes across reports may reflect wording, sample, policy context and awareness as well as changed attitudes; giving intentions are not realized donations or nonprofit revenue.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults with different service use, income, political views, charitable behavior and institutional preferences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may prefer provider-neutral service availability because they cannot distinguish nonprofit and government delivery, not because they reject either institution; perpetuity preferences do not establish grantmaking effectiveness.

related_sources.claim: Official IU release with the 2026 nonprofit-use recognition gap, confidence, political-sensitivity, provider-role, giving and foundation-horizon findings.
Full report landing page referenced by IU; retrieval was not required for the bounded public-release record.

boundary: This record identifies a nonprofit recognition, public-service legitimacy and institutional-design subtheme. It does not establish nonprofit service quality, unmet need, causal trust or political effects, realized giving, provider superiority, subgroup inequality, or a harmonized 2023–2026 trend; the public release omits the survey sample size and full methods.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Indiana University release was reviewed for the September 25, 2026 date, report title, nonprofit-use recognition gap, confidence, political-sensitivity, sector-direction uncertainty, provider-role comparison, charitable-deduction comparison and foundation-perpetuity preference.
